item.title: Kubernetes workload identity: service account tokens or Pod Certificates?
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Kubernetes 1.37 made Pod Certificates and Cluster Trust Bundles GA. How they compare with service account tokens, when to use each, and how to roll out mTLS identity.
item.content:encoded:
For years the built-in answer to 'who is this workload?' in Kubernetes was a service account token. Kubernetes 1.37 made the foundations of a second answer generally available: X.509 certificates issued to Pods. The two solve overlapping problems with different security properties.

Every service that calls another service has to prove who it is. Inside Kubernetes, the default proof has been a service account token, a signed JWT that the kubelet mounts into the Pod and keeps fresh2. It works well, which is why it underpins workload identity federation with the major cloud providers1. It also has one structural weakness, and Kubernetes 1.37 shipped a GA foundation for addressing it.

The problem with bearer tokens

Service account JWTs are bearer tokens: whoever has the token is the identity it names. To authenticate to a peer you must hand it a copy, which means the peer could replay it. Kubernetes reduces the risk by binding tokens to time, audience and objects, but the Kubernetes blog is candid that none of these are complete defences1.

The alternative is a proof-of-possession credential, where you prove you hold a secret without sending it. The most widely deployed form is the X.509 certificate used in TLS: the private key stays in the workload, and only a signature and the certificate cross the wire1.

How Pod Certificates work

A Pod requests certificates through projected volume sources in its spec13. When the Pod is scheduled, the kubelet generates a private key, creates a PodCertificateRequest addressed to a named signer, and waits for the signer controller to issue a certificate chain. The kubelet writes the key and certificate into the container, alongside trust anchors collected from matching Cluster Trust Bundles, and refreshes everything before it expires1.

Two details matter in practice. Rotation is automatic and frequent: signers eventually shipped in core are expected to issue certificates with a maximum lifetime of 24 hours, and other signers are capped at 91 days, so applications must reload credentials when files change. And security checks sit in the API server, where node restriction stops a compromised node requesting certificates for Pods not scheduled to it1.

Side by side

Service account tokensPod Certificates
Credential typeBearer JWTX.509 certificate with a private key kept in the Pod
Replay if interceptedPossible within the token's bindingsNot without the private key
Best forCalling cloud APIs and services that accept federated JWTsService-to-service mTLS inside and across clusters
Ecosystem supportVery broad todayGrowing; signers are pluggable
SignerBuilt into the control planeThird-party or custom at 1.37; built-in signers expected later
Application effortRead a file, send a headerConfigure TLS and handle frequent rotation

The blog expects at least two built-in signers over time: one for server TLS certificates matching Service DNS names, and one for SPIFFE client certificates that fill the role service account tokens play today1. SPIFFE defines a standard identity format and verifiable identity documents for workloads, which makes these identities portable across platforms4.

Use tokens to talk to clouds and APIs that expect them. Use certificates for service-to-service trust you control. Most platforms will run both for years.

How I'd roll it out

  1. Map current identity flows: which services call which, with what credential, and where tokens are forwarded rather than validated.
  2. Pick a signer strategy. Until built-in signers arrive, choose a maintained signer or your existing PKI, and decide who owns the root of trust.
  3. Start with internal mTLS between a few high-value services, using credential bundles so rotation is a single file reload.
  4. Test rotation deliberately. With lifetimes as short as a day, an application that only reads its certificate at start-up will fail.
  5. Enforce with policy: require certificate sources for services that handle sensitive data, using admission policies and the isolation model in Kubernetes multi-tenancy.
  6. Keep tokens where they fit, especially for cloud federation, and stop forwarding them between services, the same anti-pattern described in securing MCP servers.

item.title: Migrating to stateless MCP: a playbook for the 2026-07-28 specification
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: The MCP 2026-07-28 spec removed sessions and the handshake. A playbook for migrating servers, gateways and clients: state handles, MRTR, headers, caching and auth changes.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026-07-28 Model Context Protocol specification turned a stateful, bidirectional protocol into a stateless request and response one. That is good news for anyone running MCP servers at scale, and a real migration for anyone who built on sessions, server-initiated requests or long-lived streams.

Most early MCP servers were built like chat connections: a client connected, shook hands, held a session open and the server pushed requests back when it needed something. That worked on a laptop. It worked less well behind a load balancer, in serverless runtimes, or anywhere a connection could drop. The 2026-07-28 specification addresses that head on1.

What changed, in one table

BeforeFrom 2026-07-28Why it matters
initialize handshake and Mcp-Session-IdRemoved; each request carries protocol version and client capabilities in _metaAny request can land on any instance2
Capabilities learned at connect timeOptional server/discover call that servers must implementUp-front version selection when clients want it2
Server-initiated elicitation, sampling and roots requestsMulti Round-Trip Requests: the server returns input_required and the client retries with answersNo held-open bidirectional stream3
Method and tool names only in the JSON bodyMcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers required on Streamable HTTPGateways route and authorise on headers4
List results with no freshness hintsttlMs and cacheScope, plus deterministic tool orderClient caching and stable prompt caches2
SSE resumability with Last-Event-IDRemoved; a broken stream means re-issuing the requestSimpler transport, but retries must be safe2

The release also moved Tasks into an official extension, hardened authorisation with RFC 9207 issuer validation, deprecated Dynamic Client Registration in favour of client metadata documents, and introduced a formal deprecation policy with a twelve-month minimum window1.

The playbook

1. Inventory what depends on sessions

List every server and find where it relies on connection state: per-session caches, "current project" set at connect time, server-pushed requests, resumable streams. Those are your migration items. Servers that only expose stateless tools usually need little more than an SDK upgrade.

2. Replace hidden state with explicit handles

The specification's answer to cross-call state is an explicit, server-minted handle returned by a tool and passed back as an ordinary argument2. The maintainers note this works better than transport-hidden state because the model can see the handle and thread it between tools1. Store the state behind the handle in a shared store, scoped to the user, with an expiry.

3. Rework interactive tools with MRTR

Tools that asked the user for confirmation or a missing parameter mid-call now return an interim result with resultType: "input_required"; the client gathers the answers and retries the original request with them3. Design these tools so a retry is safe, and keep any correlation data in the request state rather than server memory.

4. Make retries safe everywhere

Without stream resumability, a dropped response stream means the client re-issues the request with a new ID2. Any tool with side effects needs idempotency, the same discipline as in idempotent payment pipelines.

5. Move routing and policy to the gateway

With Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name on every Streamable HTTP request4, a gateway can rate-limit, authorise and meter per tool without parsing bodies. Plain round-robin load balancing now works. This is the natural place to enforce the controls in securing MCP servers.

6. Use the cache hints

Return a deterministic tool order and sensible ttlMs values. Stable tool lists help clients cache catalogues and keep upstream prompt caches warm, which matters for cost, as covered in prompt caching.

7. Plan the deprecations

Roots, Sampling and Logging are deprecated, with suggested migrations: pass paths through tool parameters or configuration instead of Roots, call model providers directly instead of Sampling, and use stderr or OpenTelemetry instead of protocol Logging25. Trace context now has documented conventions in _meta, which fits the approach in LLM observability.

Stateless MCP doesn't make your system stateless. It makes your state visible, which is exactly where an auditor, an SRE and the model all need it to be.

Sequencing for an enterprise estate

  1. Gateway first, so routing and policy work for both old and new protocol versions during the transition.
  2. High-traffic, stateless servers next: the easiest wins for scalability.
  3. Interactive and stateful servers last, with handles and MRTR designed and tested properly.
  4. Registry metadata updated to show which protocol versions each server supports, as in an enterprise MCP registry.

item.title: Characterisation on OMOP: describe your population before you predict or estimate anything
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Database profiles, cohort characterisation, treatment pathways and incidence rates on OMOP: what each tells you, how to compute them, and why they come before AI.
item.content:encoded:
Health data teams are under pressure to jump straight to prediction models and causal studies. The most useful first step is less glamorous: describing the data and the people in it. OHDSI's characterisation methods turn that into a repeatable, shareable discipline.

A familiar pattern in health data projects: the team gets access to a new OMOP database, and within a week someone is training a risk model. A month later the model behaves strangely, and the cause turns out to be something basic. Half the patients have under a year of observation, a whole drug class is missing from one source, or the "new users" are mostly people transferring in from another system.

Characterisation is how you find those things first. The Book of OHDSI describes four methods, each answering a different question1.

Four kinds of characterisation

MethodQuestion it answersTypical use
Database-levelWhat is in this database at all?Fitness for purpose, data quality, spotting gaps
Cohort characterisationWho are these people, before and after the index date?Natural history, drug utilisation, study feasibility
Treatment pathwaysWhat sequence of treatments do people receive?Treatment patterns, switching, guideline adherence
IncidenceHow often does a new outcome occur in a population?Disease burden, safety signals, baselines for models

All except database-level characterisation describe a population relative to an index date defined by a cohort. Time before the index date is baseline; the index date and after is post-index1. That is why good cohort definitions come first.

Start with the database

Before any population question, describe the database: how many people, their age distribution, how long they are observed, and how the recording of treatments, conditions and procedures changes over time. These summaries also reveal what may be missing1, which is why they pair naturally with OMOP data quality checks.

Characterise the cohort broadly

OHDSI's approach to cohort characterisation is deliberately broad: descriptive statistics across all conditions, drug and device exposures, procedures and other observations in a person's history, plus demographics at the index date. That gives a complete picture of the population and helps surface variation and missing values1. The FeatureExtraction package produces these features in a standard way, so the same characterisation runs at every site4.

The book notes that disseminating this kind of characterisation is recommended practice in the STROBE guidelines for reporting observational studies13. Practically, a baseline table is also the fastest way to check your cohort is the population you think it is.

If the baseline table surprises you, stop. The surprise is either a finding or a data problem, and both matter more than the model you were about to train.

Treatment pathways

Pathway analysis summarises the sequence of treatments people receive after a starting event, such as a diagnosis or first prescription. In a landmark study across the OHDSI network, Hripcsak and colleagues used standardised pathway analyses for type 2 diabetes, hypertension and depression, running the same analysis across many databases2. The book reports that they found metformin to be the most common diabetes medication, consistent with first-line guidance, and that 10% of diabetes patients, 24% of hypertension patients and 11% of depression patients followed a treatment pathway shared with no one else in any of the data sources1.

That last finding is a useful reminder for anyone designing clinical AI: real-world care is far more varied than guidelines suggest.

Incidence, defined precisely

Incidence measures new occurrences of an outcome in a population during a time at risk. The book defines two metrics1:

  • Incidence proportion: people in the cohort with a new outcome during the time at risk, divided by people in the cohort with time at risk.
  • Incidence rate: people with a new outcome divided by the total person-time at risk, where each person's time stops when the outcome occurs.

Most disagreements about "the rate" of something trace back to different choices of cohort, time at risk or outcome definition. Writing those down explicitly is what makes incidence comparable across sites and studies.

Where characterisation fits

  1. Database characterisation when a source joins the platform, and after every major load.
  2. Cohort characterisation before any study or model, to confirm feasibility and population.
  3. Pathways and incidence to understand current practice and baselines.
  4. Then prediction or effect estimation, with the characterisation published alongside the results.

How I can help

I design OMOP platforms where characterisation runs automatically on every load and every new cohort, so analysts and AI teams start from facts rather than assumptions. See healthcare data architecture, or analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: OpenTelemetry declarative configuration: a playbook for moving from environment variables to one reviewed file
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: OpenTelemetry's declarative configuration schema is stable. What changed, which languages support it, and a playbook for moving SDK setup from env vars to one reviewed file.
item.content:encoded:
For years, configuring OpenTelemetry SDKs meant a growing list of OTEL_ environment variables, plus code for anything they couldn't express. The declarative configuration schema is now stable. It turns telemetry setup into a versioned file that platform teams can standardise, review and roll out.

Ask a platform team how their services configure OpenTelemetry and the honest answer is usually "it depends on the service". One team sets a dozen OTEL_ variables in a Helm chart, another wires exporters in code, a third copied a sampler setting from a blog post two years ago. The result is telemetry that differs in quality across services for no good reason, and changes that require touching every repository.

OpenTelemetry's declarative configuration is designed to fix that, and the core of it is now stable.

What changed

In March 2026 the project marked key portions of the declarative configuration specification stable12:

  • The JSON schema for the data model, released as opentelemetry-configuration 1.0.03.
  • The YAML file format and the in-memory representation of the model.
  • The SDK operations to parse a file and create SDK components from it.
  • A standard environment variable, OTEL_CONFIG_FILE, to point the SDK at the file.

At the time, implementations existed in C++, Go, Java, JavaScript and PHP, with .NET and Python under way, and the Collector used the Go implementation for its own internal telemetry1. Since then, the Java Spring Boot starter has added support from version 2.26.0, embedding the same schema in application.yaml4.

Why it matters

Environment variables are flat. They can name an exporter endpoint, but struggle with a pipeline: several processors, different exporters per signal, views that drop noisy attributes, a sampler with rules. Anything beyond them meant code, or for the Java agent a separate extension jar4. The declarative schema describes the whole SDK pipeline as a tree, in the same shape the SDK runs5:

file_format: "1.0"
resource:
  attributes:
    - name: service.name
      value: checkout
tracer_provider:
  processors:
    - batch:
        exporter:
          otlp_http:
            endpoint: ${OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT:-http://collector:4318/v1/traces}

Environment variable substitution keeps the parts that genuinely vary per environment out of the file, while everything else becomes a reviewable artefact.

Telemetry configuration is platform policy. It belongs in one reviewed file per service type, not scattered across Helm values and application code.

The playbook

1. Inventory what you have

List how each service configures its SDK today: environment variables, code, agent flags. You will usually find a few patterns that cover most services, and a long tail of one-offs.

2. Check language support

Support varies by language and by feature. The project tracks it in the specification compliance matrix and the configuration repository's language support status13. Start with the languages where support is mature in your stack.

3. Write a small set of standard files

Create a baseline per service type, such as web API, worker and batch job, covering resource attributes, exporters to your Collector gateway, batching, sampling and views. Keep secrets and endpoints as substitutions.

4. Ship the file with the platform, not the app

Mount it from a ConfigMap or bake it into base images, and set OTEL_CONFIG_FILE in your deployment templates. Teams inherit good defaults without copying settings.

5. Validate in CI

The model is defined by a JSON schema, so files can be validated before they ship3. Add the check to the same pipeline that enforces admission policies.

6. Migrate service by service

Run the declarative file alongside existing settings in a non-production environment, compare the telemetry produced, then switch. Pay attention to resource attributes and sampling, where small differences change dashboards and costs.

7. Plan for deprecations

The project intends to deprecate environment variables that don't interoperate well with declarative configuration, while making clear that deprecation is not deletion16. Moving now avoids a rushed migration later.

Where to be careful

  • Precedence. Understand how the file interacts with remaining environment variables in each language before assuming one wins.
  • Instrumentation configuration. The API for configuring instrumentation through the model was out of scope for the initial stabilisation1; check what your language supports.
  • Runtime changes. Dynamic configuration, changing telemetry without a restart, is still being designed1.
  • Stability is per language. A stable schema doesn't mean every SDK implementation is stable yet; follow the same approach as stable by default.

item.title: Keeping secrets out of Terraform state: a checklist for platform teams
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Terraform state has long held plaintext secrets. Ephemeral values and write-only arguments now keep them out. A checklist to find exposure, migrate safely and harden state.
item.content:encoded:
Most organisations using Terraform have database passwords, API keys or private keys sitting in state files, often in plaintext. For years that was simply how Terraform worked. Since versions 1.10 and 1.11 it doesn't have to be, but the fix needs deliberate migration.

Ask a platform team where their production database password lives and the answer is usually "in the secrets manager". Ask where else it lives and the honest answer is often "in the Terraform state file, in plaintext, readable by anyone with access to the state bucket". That was the default for years: a secret read through a data source or set on a resource ended up in both plan and state16.

What changed

VersionFeatureWhat it does
1.10Ephemeral values and resourcesFetch or generate values during a run without persisting them in plan or state14
1.11Write-only argumentsPass ephemeral values to managed resources; never stored in plan or state2

Together they close the gap: a secret can be read from a secrets manager ephemerally and handed to a resource through a write-only argument, without ever landing in state23. There is one catch. Because Terraform never stores the value, it can't detect when it changes. Write-only arguments are paired with a version argument that you increment to trigger an update, and only the version is stored2. Support also depends on each provider, resource by resource35.

"Sensitive" hides a value from your screen. "Ephemeral" and "write-only" keep it out of the file. Only the second protects you if the state bucket leaks.

1. Find the exposure

  • Inventory every state file and who can read it, including CI service accounts and old backends nobody uses.
  • Search state for secret-bearing attributes: passwords, private keys, tokens, connection strings.
  • List data sources that read from secrets managers; each one is copying a secret into state today.
  • Treat any secret that has ever been in state as potentially exposed to everyone with state access.

2. Upgrade the toolchain

  • Move to Terraform 1.11 or later so both features are available2.
  • Upgrade providers and check their documentation for ephemeral resources and write-only arguments on the resources you use.
  • If you run OpenTofu, check its equivalent features and version support separately; the choice is covered in OpenTofu or Terraform.

3. Migrate resource by resource

  • Replace secret-reading data sources with ephemeral resources where the provider offers them.
  • Switch resources to write-only arguments for passwords and keys, with a version argument for rotation.
  • Rotate the secret as part of the migration. Moving to write-only stops future storage; it doesn't undo past exposure.
  • Better still, let the platform generate and manage the secret itself, such as a managed database credential stored in the cloud's secrets manager, so Terraform never handles it.
  • Update shared modules first, using the patterns in Terraform module design, so every consumer benefits.

4. Harden state anyway

  • Encrypt state at rest with customer-managed keys and restrict decrypt permissions.
  • Limit state read access to the pipelines that need it; humans rarely do.
  • Enable versioning and access logging on the state backend, and alert on unusual reads.
  • Keep plan files out of CI artefacts and logs, or apply the same controls to them.

5. Keep it from regressing

  • Add a policy check in CI that flags secret-bearing attributes set through normal arguments, and secret-reading data sources.
  • Document the rotation process using version arguments, so it's routine rather than tribal knowledge.
  • Include state access in access reviews and in your SOC 2 evidence; it is often the broadest secret access in the company.

item.title: SLOs and error budgets for small teams: field notes on making reliability a decision, not a debate
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: SLOs and error budgets work for small teams too. How to choose SLOs, write an error budget policy, alert on burn rate and use the budget to settle priorities.
item.content:encoded:
In a small company, the argument between shipping features and fixing reliability usually gets settled by whoever is loudest that week. Service level objectives and error budgets turn it into a rule everyone agreed in advance. The Google SRE material is written for large organisations, but the core ideas scale down well.

A familiar scene in a growing company: a bad week of incidents, a tense meeting, a decision to "focus on stability" for a sprint, and then feature pressure creeps back until the next bad week. Nobody is wrong. Product wants to ship, engineering wants to stop firefighting, and there is no shared definition of "reliable enough" to settle the question.

Error budgets were designed for exactly this. The original Google SRE book frames reliability as a target to be chosen, not maximised, because every extra nine costs something5. Once the target is agreed, the gap between it and perfection is a budget the team is allowed to spend.

Start smaller than you think

Small teams fail at SLOs by trying to cover everything. Two or three objectives on the user journeys that matter most is enough to start:

  • Availability of the core API or page: the proportion of valid requests that succeed.
  • Latency for the same journey: the proportion of requests faster than a threshold users would notice.
  • Freshness or correctness for data products: the proportion of runs completed on time.

Measure at the edge closest to users, such as the load balancer or gateway, and set the first targets from what you achieved over the last month. The Workbook recommends writing the SLOs down with owners, approvers and review dates, and its example document gives each objective its own budget of 100% minus the target14.

Write the policy before you need it

The SLO is a number; the policy is what makes it matter. The Workbook says a policy should state the actions taken when the budget is exhausted and a clear escalation path for disagreements1. Its example policy is a useful template2:

TriggerExample action
Budget exhausted over the preceding four weeksHalt changes and releases other than P0 issues and security fixes until back within SLO
A single incident consumes over 20% of the four-week budgetPostmortem with at least one P0 action item
One class of outage consumes over 20% of the quarterly budgetA P0 item in next quarter's plan
Budget spent by causes outside the team's controlListed exceptions, such as company-wide network problems

For a small company, a softer version often works better: rather than halting all releases, the next sprint's capacity goes to reliability work until the budget recovers. What matters is that product and engineering leadership sign it together, before the next bad week.

The error budget's real value is political, not technical. It replaces an argument about feelings with a rule both sides agreed when they were calm.

Alert on burn rate, not on errors

Paging on every error spike burns out small on-call rotations fast. The Workbook's guidance is to alert on how quickly the budget is being consumed, combining multiple time windows and burn rates so that fast, severe problems page someone while slow leaks become tickets3. With two or three SLOs, that typically means a handful of alerts in total, each of which genuinely matters.

The telemetry comes from the same pipeline as everything else; the OpenTelemetry Collector patterns make it straightforward to compute SLIs centrally.

What changes once it's running

  • Prioritisation gets easier. Budget remaining means ship; budget gone means fix. The weekly debate shrinks to a glance at a dashboard.
  • Postmortems get sharper. Budget consumed per incident is a better severity measure than whoever shouted loudest, and pairs well with the practices in AI incident postmortems.
  • Delivery metrics gain context. DORA metrics say how fast you ship; error budgets say whether the speed is affordable.
  • Customer conversations improve. An SLO you actually meet is a far better basis for an SLA than an aspiration.

Mistakes to avoid

  1. Targets nobody would notice missing. If users wouldn't feel a breach, the SLO is measuring the wrong thing.
  2. 100% targets. They leave no budget, so every change becomes a violation5.
  3. A policy without a signature from product. Then it is an engineering wish, not an agreement.
  4. Never revisiting. Review targets quarterly, as the Workbook's document template expects4.

How I can help

item.title: Speculative decoding for private LLMs: faster tokens without changing the answers
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM generation without changing outputs. How it works, when it helps on self-hosted models in vLLM, which method to choose, and how to measure it.
item.content:encoded:
Self-hosting a model gives you control over data and cost, and often a latency problem. Speculative decoding is one of the few optimisations that makes generation faster without changing what the model outputs. It also has a narrower sweet spot than its benchmarks suggest.

A common moment in private LLM projects: the model runs on your own GPUs, quality is acceptable, and users complain that answers stream slowly. Buying more hardware raises throughput but barely changes how quickly each token appears for one user. Quantisation and smaller models change the outputs. Speculative decoding is attractive because it does neither.

How it works

Generating text one token at a time leaves a large model's GPU mostly waiting on memory, not compute. Speculative decoding uses that slack. A cheap proposer guesses the next few tokens; the large target model checks all of them in one parallel pass; accepted tokens are kept, and generation continues from the first rejection1.

The original Google Research paper showed this can sample from the target model's distribution exactly, so outputs are unchanged, and reported 2 to 3 times faster generation on T5-XXL with existing models and no retraining1. In practice, floating-point differences in batched GPU execution mean byte-identical outputs are likely rather than guaranteed.

Speculative decoding trades spare compute for latency. If your GPUs have no spare compute, there is nothing to trade.

The proposer options

MethodHow it proposesTrade-off
Draft modelA smaller model from the same familyGood acceptance; extra memory and a model to manage
EAGLE familyA light head trained on the target model's internal featuresStrong speedups; needs a head trained for your exact model
MTPMulti-token prediction layers built into some modelsNo separate model, where the base model supports it
N-gram / suffixCopies likely continuations from the prompt or earlier outputNo training; helps most when output repeats input

The current vLLM documentation summarises it this way: model-based methods such as EAGLE, MTP and draft models give the best latency reduction, while n-gram and suffix decoding give modest speedups without adding much work during peak traffic3. The EAGLE-3 paper reports speedups of up to 6.5 times in its experiments and argues its design lets the draft head benefit from more training data2. The vLLM project also maintains a Speculators library for training draft models that run in vLLM4.

When it helps, and when it doesn't

vLLM describes speculative decoding as aimed at reducing inter-token latency for memory-bound workloads at medium to low request rates3. That sentence is the whole story:

  • Interactive assistants with modest concurrency: good fit. Each user sees faster streaming.
  • Code editing, document revision, extraction: often good for n-gram methods, because the output repeats large parts of the input.
  • High-throughput batch jobs: weak fit. The GPU is already saturated, and verification work competes with real requests.
  • Peak hours on shared clusters: gains can fall as load rises, which is why the cheaper methods appeal.

Older vLLM releases also carried caveats, such as incompatibility with pipeline parallelism and inconsistent latency gains across datasets5. Check the documentation for your exact version rather than relying on a blog post's configuration.

How I'd evaluate it

  1. Replay real traffic, not a benchmark prompt set. Acceptance rate depends heavily on what your users ask and how your prompts are built.
  2. Measure the right latencies: time to first token, inter-token latency and end-to-end time, at your real concurrency, using the telemetry in LLM observability.
  3. Track acceptance rate and tune the number of speculative tokens; low acceptance means wasted verification.
  4. Check outputs on your evaluation set to confirm nothing changed that matters.
  5. Compare with alternatives. Prompt caching and routing easy requests to smaller models may deliver more for less effort.
  6. Decide per workload. Enable it for interactive endpoints and leave batch endpoints alone, using the serving patterns in vLLM inference serving.

item.title: Real-world evidence on OMOP: comparing five study designs for treatment effects
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Cohort method, self-controlled cohort, case-control, case-crossover and self-controlled case series compared: what each answers, its main bias, and how to choose.
item.content:encoded:
Asking 'does this drug cause that outcome?' of observational data is easy. Getting an answer you can defend is not. The OHDSI community implements five main designs for population-level estimation, each with a different way of approximating what would have happened otherwise, and each with its own blind spots.

Pharma medical affairs, payers, health systems and regulators all want the same thing from real-world data: evidence about what treatments actually do outside trials. The data, mostly claims and electronic health records, is plentiful. The hard part is design. Every observational study is an attempt to estimate a counterfactual, what would have happened to these patients without the exposure or with a different one, from data that only records what did happen1.

The OHDSI community implements five main designs for this as open-source R packages in its Methods Library, all running on OMOP data13. Knowing what each one assumes is the difference between evidence and a confident-looking chart.

The five designs at a glance

DesignComparesMain strengthMain vulnerability
Cohort method (new user)New users of target vs new users of comparatorEmulates a trial; rich diagnosticsUnmeasured confounding between groups
Self-controlled cohortExposed time vs time just before exposureNo between-person confoundingBaseline risk differing between periods
Case-controlExposure in people with vs without the outcomeEfficient for rare outcomesChoice of controls
Case-crossoverExposure at outcome time vs an earlier control timeCases are their own controlsTrends in exposure over time
Self-controlled case seriesOutcome rate in exposed vs all unexposed timeNo between-person confoundingTime-varying confounding; outcomes that end observation

All rows are drawn from the descriptions in The Book of OHDSI1.

Cohort method: emulating a trial

The new-user cohort design compares people who start the target treatment with people who start a comparator, and follows them for a defined time-at-risk. It is defined by five choices: target cohort, comparator cohort, outcome cohort, time-at-risk and model1.

The central problem is that patients on different treatments differ. OHDSI's preferred adjustment is a propensity score fitted with large-scale regularised regression over many generic characteristics, typically 10,000 to 100,000 of them, rather than a hand-picked list1. The design comes with diagnostics: preference score distributions to check the groups overlap, and covariate balance after adjustment, where some guidelines recommend standardised differences below 0.114.

The book is clear that this is inherently a comparative design. Comparing a treatment with no treatment is hard because a comparable unexposed group is difficult to define; an active comparator for the same indication is preferred1.

Self-controlled designs: people as their own controls

Three designs avoid between-person comparison altogether. The self-controlled cohort compares outcome rates during exposure with the time just before. The case-crossover design asks whether exposure was more common just before the outcome than at an earlier control time; because the outcome always comes later, it can be biased by exposure trends, which the case-time-control variant addresses. The self-controlled case series compares the outcome rate during exposed time with all unexposed time, before, between and after exposures1.

These designs are robust to confounding by stable characteristics such as genetics or chronic conditions, but vulnerable to things that change over time, such as age, season or disease progression1. The self-controlled case series also assumes the end of observation is independent of the outcome, which can fail for fatal outcomes such as stroke; an extension exists to correct for that15.

No design is assumption-free. Choose the one whose weaknesses matter least for your question, then test it on questions where you already know the answer.

Case-control: efficient, but fragile

Case-control studies compare exposure in people with the outcome against people without it, often matching on age and sex and sometimes nesting within a subgroup such as patients with the relevant indication1. They are efficient for rare outcomes, but results depend heavily on how controls are selected.

How I'd choose and validate

  1. Write the question precisely as cohorts and time windows, as in OMOP cohort definitions.
  2. Default to the new-user cohort design with an active comparator for comparative effectiveness, because its diagnostics make problems visible.
  3. Use self-controlled designs for acute outcomes after transient exposures, such as vaccine or short-course drug safety, where timing is sharp.
  4. Run negative controls. Outcomes believed not to be caused by the exposure reveal residual bias; the book's method validity chapter covers this and empirical calibration2.
  5. Replicate across databases through the federated network approach, after data quality checks at each site.
  6. Keep estimation and prediction separate. Causal questions and prediction models need different designs and different validation.

item.title: Fine-tuning a foundation model? When the EU AI Act makes you a general-purpose AI provider
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: EU AI Act rules for general-purpose AI models now have enforcement behind them. When fine-tuning makes you a GPAI provider, what the Code of Practice asks, and what to document.
item.content:encoded:
Most companies building on foundation models assume the EU's general-purpose AI rules are for the labs. Usually they are. But the Commission's guidelines draw a line where heavy modification turns a downstream builder into a provider, and since August 2026 the AI Office can enforce those rules.

Picture a scale-up that takes an open-weight model, continues pre-training it on a large domain corpus, fine-tunes it further and offers it to customers across Europe. Is it a deployer of someone else's model, or the provider of a new general-purpose AI model? Under the EU AI Act the answer changes the paperwork considerably, and it now carries enforcement risk.

This is an architect's reading of public guidance and law firm commentary, not legal advice.

Where things stand

The AI Act's obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models have applied since 2 August 2025. The Commission said the AI Office was preparing its compliance assessments ahead of enforcement of those rules from August 20262. A Cloud Security Alliance research note published on 3 August 2026 summarised the AI Office's powers as including requests for documentation, model evaluations, corrective measures and fines7.

Alongside the law sit two practical instruments. The GPAI Code of Practice, published on 10 July 2025, has three chapters: transparency, copyright, and safety and security. The first two give all GPAI providers a way to demonstrate compliance with Article 53; the third applies only to providers of models with systemic risk under Article 5516. The transparency chapter includes a Model Documentation Form1. The Commission also finalised a template for the public summary of training data5.

The line between deployer and provider

The Commission's guidelines on GPAI providers address downstream modification directly. As summarised by commentators34:

  • An indicative criterion is whether the training compute used for the modification exceeds one third of the compute used to train the original model.
  • If the original compute isn't known, one third of the threshold for presuming a model is general-purpose is used instead.
  • Minor changes typically don't make you a provider.
  • If you do become a provider, your obligations generally concern the modification: documentation, training data summary and copyright policy covering the additional compute and data. Modifying a model with systemic risk brings the full systemic-risk obligations.
What you doLikely position
Prompting, RAG, tool use, agents on a hosted modelNot modifying the model
Light fine-tuning or adapters on modest dataTypically a minor change
Large continued pre-training or extensive fine-tuningCheck the compute ratio carefully
Modifying a model already classed as systemic-riskGet specific legal advice early

Most teams are nowhere near the line. The ones that are usually know it, because they are spending serious money on GPUs. That spend should come with a compliance budget.

Why this matters even if you are well below it

First, customers ask. In enterprise procurement, "we use RAG, not fine-tuning" is a much easier answer with evidence behind it. Second, upstream providers' documentation flows down to you: the Model Documentation Form exists partly so downstream providers can understand the models they build on1. Third, the same records support obligations that apply to your AI systems regardless of the model rules, such as the literacy duty in Article 4 and the timeline in the Digital Omnibus roadmap.

What I'd put in place

  1. Log training compute for every model you train or tune, with the method used to estimate it. It's cheap to capture at the time and very hard to reconstruct later.
  2. Keep a model lineage record: base model and version, upstream documentation received, datasets, licences and changes. The supply chain practices in AI model supply chain security overlap heavily.
  3. Document data provenance and copyright handling for any data you train on, including how rights reservations are respected.
  4. Prefer adaptation over retraining where it meets the need. RAG and lighter tuning are usually cheaper as well as simpler to govern; see long context vs RAG.
  5. Map once, reuse often. Tie these records into a framework such as ISO 42001 so the same evidence serves EU, US and Gulf requirements.

item.title: Kafka queues are production-ready: when share groups can replace a separate message broker
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Apache Kafka 4.2 made queues (share groups) production-ready. How they differ from consumer groups, which workloads they fit, and when a separate message broker still makes sense.
item.content:encoded:
Many platforms run Kafka for event streams and a second system for work queues, because Kafka's consumer groups tie each partition to one consumer. Kafka 4.2 made share groups, its queue semantics, production-ready. For some teams, that means one less system to run.

A familiar architecture: Kafka carries business events between services and into the lakehouse, while RabbitMQ, SQS or a database-backed job table handles background work such as sending emails, generating documents or calling a model. Two systems, two sets of operational skills, two places where messages can get stuck. The reason was structural. Kafka's consumer groups assign each partition to exactly one consumer, so you cannot scale workers beyond the partition count, and one slow message holds up everything behind it.

What changed

KIP-932, "Queues for Kafka", introduced share groups. Kafka 4.0, the first release to run only in KRaft mode without ZooKeeper, offered them as early access45. The 4.2.0 release announcement describes Kafka Queues as production-ready, adding a RENEW acknowledgement type, adaptive batching in the share coordinator, limits on fetched record counts, and lag metrics13.

Consumer groups versus share groups

The Kafka documentation describes share groups as an alternative to consumer groups: consumers share a topic's records without each partition being tied to one consumer, records are acknowledged individually, and delivery attempts are counted. It suggests them for workloads that process records one at a time rather than as an ordered stream2.

Consumer groupShare group
AssignmentEach partition to one consumerRecords shared across consumers
Scaling limitNumber of partitionsNot tied to partition count
Progress trackingOffset per partitionAcknowledgement per record
RetriesBuilt by the applicationDelivery attempts counted by Kafka
OrderingPreserved within a partitionNot the design goal
Best forEvent streams, CDC, aggregationsIndependent tasks: jobs, notifications, AI calls

If the order of records matters, use a consumer group. If each record is an independent piece of work, a share group is now a real option.

Where it fits well

  • AI and enrichment workloads. Calling a model for each document or record is slow and variable. Share groups let you add workers to match throughput without repartitioning, and a slow call doesn't block the rest.
  • Fan-out jobs from existing events. If the events already land in Kafka, for example from change data capture, processing them as tasks without copying them to another broker removes a hop.
  • Bursty background work, where worker count needs to swing widely during the day, combined with autoscaling like that in Kubernetes scale-to-zero.

Where a separate broker still wins

  • No Kafka today. Adopting Kafka just for a work queue is rarely worth it. A managed queue is simpler.
  • Complex routing. Topic exchanges, header-based routing and per-message priorities remain stronger in dedicated brokers.
  • Strict ordering with parallelism. If you need per-key order and parallel processing, keyed consumer groups remain the right model.
  • Small clusters. Share groups store state in an internal topic that defaults to three replicas, so clusters with fewer than three brokers must adjust internal replication settings first2.

How I'd adopt it

  1. Get to a current release. Share groups need KRaft-based Kafka 4.x; plan the ZooKeeper migration first if you haven't5. Run the latest 4.2 patch release rather than 4.2.0.
  2. Pick one queue workload that already consumes from Kafka and has idempotent processing, using the patterns in idempotent pipelines. Per-record acknowledgement still means at-least-once delivery.
  3. Decide what happens after the last attempt. Route repeatedly failing records somewhere a person will see them.
  4. Monitor share-group lag with the new metrics and alert on it, as you would queue depth1.
  5. Check your managed service. Hosted Kafka offerings adopt new features and metrics at different speeds.
  6. Retire the old queue only after a full cycle of peak load and incident handling on the new one.

item.title: Running an enterprise MCP registry: a playbook for governed tool discovery
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: The official MCP Registry is designed to feed subregistries. A playbook for running a private enterprise MCP registry: curation, namespaces, approvals and client rollout.
item.content:encoded:
Once a few teams adopt MCP, the question shifts from 'how do I build a server?' to 'which servers are we allowed to use?'. The MCP Registry was designed with that in mind: a public upstream that organisations can mirror, filter and extend with their own private servers.

A typical enterprise MCP adoption follows a pattern. A few engineers connect assistants to useful servers. A platform team builds internal servers for the CRM, the data warehouse and the ticketing system. Within months there are dozens of servers, nobody knows which are approved, and security finds a community server with broad file system access on a developer laptop. The fix is not to ban MCP. It is to give people a catalogue of servers they're allowed to use.

How the MCP Registry is designed

The official MCP Registry launched in preview in September 2025 as an open catalogue of publicly available servers14. Three design choices matter for enterprises:

  • Metadata, not code. Entries describe servers and point to packages in existing registries such as npm, PyPI and Docker Hub12.
  • Verified namespaces. Server names use a reverse-DNS format, such as io.github.username/server or com.example/server, tied to a verified GitHub account or domain2. That gives you a basis for trusting who published what.
  • Built to be extended. The registry and its API specification are open source, so others can build compatible subregistries that pull from it, filter it and add their own servers13.

The registry remains in preview, and its documentation warns that breaking changes or data resets may occur before general availability2. Build against it, but pin and mirror what you depend on.

The playbook

1. Decide what "approved" means

Write down the criteria before choosing tools: publisher verified, source available, package signed or pinned, permissions documented, data classification of what it touches, and an internal owner. The controls in securing MCP servers make a good starting checklist.

2. Stand up a private subregistry

Run a registry that implements the same API, so clients that understand the official registry can use yours35. Servers on internal hostnames or private package feeds belong here, not in the public registry2.

3. Mirror, don't proxy

Pull public entries into a staging area, review them, then promote approved versions. Pin to specific package versions so an upstream update can't change what your users run without review. This is the same discipline as AI supply chain security.

4. Enrich entries with your context

Add what the public registry can't know: owner, data classification, allowed user groups, required auth extension, and a link to the review record. Tool annotations and UI capabilities, covered in MCP Apps and tool annotations, should be part of the review.

5. Point clients at it

Configure managed IDEs and assistants to discover servers from your registry, and where clients support it, block unapproved sources. A catalogue nobody is pointed at is just documentation.

6. Tie it to identity

Approval should map to who can use a server. Pair the registry with the enterprise authorisation patterns in MCP extensions, so access is granted through your identity provider rather than per-server credentials.

7. Measure and prune

Track which servers are used, by whom and how often, using the telemetry approach in LLM observability. Retire servers without owners or usage, and re-review on major version changes.

A registry turns MCP from a collection of personal integrations into a platform. The governance lives in the promotion step, not the protocol.

Common mistakes

  • Treating the public registry as an allow-list. Listing proves a verified namespace, not safety.
  • Floating versions. "Latest" from upstream means unreviewed code on every laptop.
  • No owner per server. Internal servers without owners become the next unpatched dependency.
  • Registry without enforcement. If clients can still add any server, the registry is advisory only.

item.title: The UAE's new Federal Authority for AI and Data: what it means for technology teams
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: The UAE has merged its AI office, digital government and data office into one federal authority. What has been announced, what is still unknown, and how I'd prepare.
item.content:encoded:
In June 2026 the UAE created a single federal body for AI, data governance and digital government. This week Dubai set new targets for its AI campus. For companies building or selling AI in the Emirates, the institutional map is consolidating, and that changes who sets the standards you'll be measured against.

For years, AI and data policy in the UAE was spread across several bodies: an AI office within the federal government, the digital government function inside the telecoms regulator, a data office, and emirate-level and free zone authorities alongside them. Teams working here learned to ask "which regulator?" before "which rule?". That is starting to change.

This is an architect's reading of public announcements and law firm commentary, not legal advice.

What was announced

In June 2026 the UAE approved the establishment of the Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data, reporting to the Cabinet, as a unified national body for data governance, artificial intelligence and digital government12. Commentary reports that it brings together three existing functions13:

Previous bodyWhat it covered
Artificial Intelligence OfficeNational AI strategy and programmes
TDRA Information and Digital Government SectorFederal digital government services and standards
Emirates Data OfficeNational data governance

The mandate described in commentary covers the national AI strategy, government data governance, and standards and compliance across federal entities13. By October, reporting on the UAE's AI programme was already framing the authority as the body bringing national data, AI and digital government systems together6.

This week: Dubai's AI campus targets

On 26 October, during the Dubai AI Festival, Dubai approved new targets for its AI campus: more than 1,000 AI companies and over 5,000 specialised jobs by 203045. Together with federal consolidation, the direction is clear: one national voice on AI and data standards, and emirate-level competition to host the companies building on them.

Consolidation usually means fewer, clearer standards, applied more consistently. Teams that have been relying on ambiguity should plan for less of it.

What we don't know yet

  • Private sector reach. The described mandate centres on federal entities. How far its standards will extend to private companies, directly or through procurement, is not yet clear.
  • Interaction with free zones. DIFC and ADGM have their own data protection regimes, including DIFC Regulation 10 on AI systems. How federal AI standards will sit alongside them remains to be seen.
  • Data protection supervision. The federal PDPL continues to apply. Which body leads on its AI-related aspects will become clearer through guidance.
  • Health data. Sector rules, such as those in the UAE health data law, remain in place.

The regional pattern

Saudi Arabia went down this path earlier, with the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority as a single body for data and AI7, alongside its own data protection law covered in Saudi PDPL and cross-border AI. A combined data and AI authority tends to treat data governance and AI governance as one discipline. Architecturally, that's right: most AI risk is data risk.

How I'd prepare

  1. Map your current obligations by entity and location: federal PDPL, free zone regimes, sector rules, and where your models and data actually run, as discussed in UAE AI infrastructure.
  2. Build governance on a recognised framework, such as ISO 42001 or the NIST AI RMF, so national standards become a mapping exercise.
  3. If you sell to government, expect federal data and AI standards to appear in procurement first. Keep an AI system inventory and data lineage ready to evidence.
  4. Unify data and AI governance internally. If the regulator treats them as one discipline, a separate AI committee disconnected from data owners will struggle.
  5. Watch for guidance from the new authority and plan a quarterly review of your mapping.

item.title: SKOS or OWL? Choosing the right model for enterprise taxonomies and ontologies
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: SKOS and OWL are both W3C standards for knowledge models, and they solve different problems. When to use each, how to combine them, and the most common enterprise mistake.
item.content:encoded:
Enterprise ontology programmes often stall on a modelling question disguised as a tooling one: should the product taxonomy, the risk register or the clinical code list be an OWL ontology or a SKOS vocabulary? The answer is usually both, for different jobs.

Every organisation already has knowledge models. They're in spreadsheets of product categories, SharePoint term stores, code lists in the data warehouse and the folder structure of the document system. When an ontology or knowledge graph programme starts, one of the first decisions is how to represent these formally. Two W3C standards dominate the conversation, and choosing the wrong one for a given job is a common reason programmes lose a year.

Two standards, two purposes

SKOS, the Simple Knowledge Organization System, became a W3C Recommendation in 2009. It is a common data model for sharing and linking knowledge organisation systems, such as thesauri, taxonomies and classification schemes, on the web1. Its world is concepts, labels and loose relations between them.

OWL 2, the Web Ontology Language, defines classes, properties and logical axioms that reasoners can use to infer new facts and detect contradictions. Its profiles, finalised in their second edition in 2012, trade expressiveness for tractable reasoning3.

The SKOS designers were explicit that SKOS was not meant to compete with OWL but to complement it, offering a path to bring existing knowledge that doesn't map easily into an OWL ontology onto the semantic web5.

Side by side

SKOSOWL 2
Core unitConcept with labelsClass, property, individual
Hierarchyskos:broader: "is filed under", for navigation and retrievalrdfs:subClassOf: "every X is a Y", logical subsumption
LabelsFirst-class: preferred, alternative and hidden labels, with at most one preferred label per language1Annotations, not part of the logic
ReasoningLight; little to inferRich, with profiles tuned for scale3
Cross-scheme linksMapping properties such as exact, close and broader matches1Equivalence and subclass axioms with logical consequences
Who maintains itTaxonomists, subject experts, business ownersOntologists and data architects
Best forProduct categories, subject tags, code lists, synonyms for searchDomain models, constraints, integration semantics

The mistake that matters most

The most expensive error is treating a taxonomy hierarchy as a class hierarchy. In a product catalogue, "Garden furniture" sits under "Outdoor" and also under "Furniture". That is a filing decision, not a claim that every garden chair is, logically, an instance of "Outdoor".

SKOS is careful here. skos:broader is used only for direct hierarchical links and is not declared transitive; skos:broaderTransitive is a separate superproperty for inferring indirect links12. Converting the same hierarchy into rdfs:subClassOf makes every relation logically binding, and a reasoner will happily draw conclusions nobody intended.

If the business owner would say "it's filed under", use SKOS. If they would say "it is always a kind of", consider OWL. Most enterprise hierarchies are the first.

Choosing OWL profiles when you do need logic

Where OWL is the right tool, its profiles help match reasoning to scale34:

  • OWL 2 EL suits ontologies with very large numbers of classes and properties, with polynomial-time reasoning for core tasks. Large biomedical terminologies are the classic fit.
  • OWL 2 QL targets large volumes of instance data queried through relational databases, which suits virtual knowledge graphs over existing warehouses.
  • OWL 2 RL supports rule-based reasoning that works directly on RDF triples, practical inside many triple stores.

Choosing a profile early prevents a common failure: a model that is logically elegant and unusable at production volume.

The combined pattern I use

  1. A small OWL core for the domain: customer, product, contract, patient, asset, and the relations between them. Keep it in a tractable profile.
  2. SKOS vocabularies for classification: product categories, risk types, diagnosis groupings, document subjects. Instances in the core point to concepts through ordinary properties, such as "has category".
  3. Mappings between vocabularies using SKOS mapping properties, so a local code list can align with an industry standard without pretending they are identical.
  4. SHACL for data quality, as described in SHACL validation, because closed-world checks belong outside the open-world logic of OWL.
  5. Labels feed search and AI. SKOS alternative and hidden labels give retrieval and GraphRAG the synonyms and misspellings users actually type.

This also clarifies ownership. Business teams can maintain vocabularies in a taxonomy tool without touching the ontology, while architects govern the core. How these pieces relate to a semantic layer is covered in ontology vs knowledge graph vs semantic layer, and how clinical vocabularies are handled in practice in clinical terminologies in OMOP.

item.title: SMART on FHIR for AI apps: an authorisation checklist for clinical data access
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: AI apps that read EHR data need SMART on FHIR authorisation done properly. A checklist covering v2 granular scopes, PKCE, backend services and agent access to clinical data.
item.content:encoded:
Ambient scribes, chart summarisers and clinical agents all need to read and sometimes write EHR data. SMART on FHIR is how they should get that access. The hard questions in a health AI security review are usually about scopes, launch context and token handling, not the model.

A health AI product usually starts with a demo against a sandbox and a broad token. Then it meets a hospital's security review. The questions are rarely about the model. They are about which data the app can reach, on whose behalf, for how long, and how anyone would know if it reached further than it should.

SMART on FHIR answers most of those questions if it is used properly. This checklist is what I work through when designing or reviewing EHR access for AI applications.

Why it matters more for AI

Traditional SMART apps show data to a clinician who is already authorised to see it. AI apps often do more: summarise a whole record, draft notes back into the chart, or run in the background across many patients. That widens both the data an app touches and the consequences of a misconfigured scope. In the US, HTI-1 also moved certified health IT from SMART v1 to the SMART App Launch 2.0 guide for the standardised patient and population API criterion, so v2 behaviour is now the baseline buyers expect6. The policy side is covered in HTI-1 to HTI-5.

1. Scopes: ask for the least, precisely

  • Use v2 scope syntax. Permissions are expressed as suffixes from c, r, u, d and s. patient/Observation.rs grants read and search on the patient's observations; patient/Observation.cu grants create and update1.
  • Narrow with search parameters. v2 allows granular scopes such as Observation access limited to the vital-signs category15. A sepsis model that only needs vitals and labs shouldn't hold a token for psychotherapy notes.
  • Prefer patient/ over user/ and system/ wherever the use case is about one patient in context.
  • Separate read and write. If the AI drafts notes, consider a distinct, reviewable write path rather than giving the summariser create rights.
  • Check what the server actually supports. Servers advertise capabilities in their SMART configuration5; don't assume granular scopes are enforced everywhere.

2. Launch and token handling

  • PKCE with S256, always. The specification says all SMART apps shall support PKCE, servers shall support S256 and shall not support the plain method2.
  • Use EHR launch for in-workflow AI, so the patient and encounter come from the EHR's launch context, not from parameters the app constructs12.
  • Request openid fhirUser so every AI action can be attributed to an identified user2.
  • Keep tokens out of the model. Access tokens belong in the integration layer, never in prompts, logs or tool arguments the model can see or echo.
  • Be deliberate about offline access. Refresh tokens extend reach well beyond the clinician's session; request them only when the use case needs it.

The model should never hold a credential. It asks a tool for data; the tool holds the token, enforces scope and logs the call.

3. Background and population workloads

  • Use SMART Backend Services for autonomous processing, such as overnight risk scoring or quality measures. It is designed for clients with pre-authorised scopes and no user in the loop3.
  • Authenticate with asymmetric keys. private_key_jwt is the specification's preferred method because no shared secret crosses the wire; clients must support RS384 and ES3844.
  • Rotate keys through a JWKS endpoint, and treat the private key with the same controls as any production secret.
  • Use bulk export for volume, as in FHIR bulk data pipelines, rather than looping single-patient queries.

4. Agents and tools

  • One tool, one scope set. If an agent reaches FHIR through MCP servers, each server should hold the narrowest token for its job, with the controls in securing MCP servers.
  • Keep patient context fixed. An agent must not be able to switch patients by changing a tool argument; patient identity comes from the launch, not the prompt. This is a key defence against prompt injection.
  • Human approval for writes. Drafted notes, orders or messages go to a clinician for review before they are committed, as in ambient scribe architectures.

5. Evidence for the security review

  • A table of every scope requested, why, and which feature uses it.
  • Audit logs linking each FHIR call to user, patient, feature and model version.
  • Token lifetimes, refresh policy and revocation procedure.
  • Results of testing with a SMART conformance tool against the target servers.
  • A data flow showing exactly where PHI goes, including any model provider, mapped to HIPAA Security Rule controls.

item.title: In-place Pod resize on Kubernetes: field notes for right-sizing without restarts
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: In-place Pod resize is stable in Kubernetes 1.35, letting CPU and memory change without recreating Pods. How it works, where it bites, and how I'd use it to cut cost.
item.content:encoded:
For years, changing a Pod's CPU or memory meant replacing the Pod. That made right-sizing disruptive, so most teams over-provisioned and left it there. With in-place resize stable since Kubernetes 1.35, the excuse is gone. The operational details still matter.

Almost every Kubernetes cost review finds the same thing: requests set generously at launch and never touched again. Teams know the numbers are wrong. They leave them because changing them used to mean rolling every Pod, and nobody wants to explain a restart to a stateful service, a long-running batch job or a model server that takes minutes to warm up.

That constraint has gone. These are notes on what changed and how I would put it to work.

What changed

In-place Pod resize arrived as alpha in Kubernetes 1.27, reached beta in 1.33 and graduated to stable in 1.3513. It makes CPU and memory requests and limits mutable on a running Pod. You send the change to the Pod's resize subresource, for example with kubectl patch --subresource resize, which needs kubectl 1.32 or later2.

Each container declares a resizePolicy per resource. NotRequired asks for the change to be applied without a restart; RestartContainer restarts that container to apply it. A common pattern in the documentation is CPU set to NotRequired and memory set to RestartContainer2.

The stable release added two things operators will notice. Memory limits can now be decreased, with the kubelet only allowing it when current usage is below the new limit, a best-effort check rather than a guarantee. And when a node can't fit every pending resize, retries are ordered by PriorityClass, then QoS class, then how long the request has waited1.

Watch the conditions, not just the spec

A resize is a request, not a guarantee. The kubelet reports progress through Pod conditions2:

ConditionReasonMeaning
PodResizePendingDeferredDoesn't fit now, might fit later; the kubelet keeps retrying
PodResizePendingInfeasibleCan never fit on this node as it stands
PodResizeInProgress(none) or ErrorAccepted and being applied; errors in actuation surface here

The practical rule: alert on long-lived PodResizePending. A spec that says 4 CPUs while the container still runs on 2 is a quiet source of confusion in incidents and cost reports alike.

The spec says what you asked for. The status says what you got. Right-sizing dashboards should read the status.

Where the VPA fits

The Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommends requests from observed usage and applies them. Its InPlaceOrRecreate update mode tries an in-place resize first and falls back to recreating the Pod when that isn't possible; the 1.35 release blog described that mode as graduating to beta15.

This is the combination that changes cost economics. Recommendations used to sit in a report because applying them was disruptive. With in-place updates they can be applied continuously, within limits you set.

Pod-level resources are next

Kubernetes 1.36 promoted in-place resize of Pod-level resources to beta, meaning a shared budget for all containers in a Pod can also change without recreating it4. That is useful for Pods with sidecars, where per-container numbers are hard to tune separately. I would treat it as beta: pilot it, but don't build a platform default on it yet.

Where it bites

  • Applications that size themselves at start-up. A runtime that reads its memory limit once, such as a JVM heap or a worker pool sized to CPU count, won't notice a change. For those, a restart policy on memory is the honest choice.
  • Memory decreases. The usage check is best-effort, so shrinking memory on a busy Pod still carries OOM risk1. Shrink gradually and watch.
  • Node fragmentation. Growing in place only works if the node has room. Busy nodes produce Deferred resizes; plan headroom or accept fallback to recreation.
  • Quotas and policy. Resizes still count against namespace quotas, and teams will need guardrails on how far they can go, enforced with admission policies in multi-tenant clusters.

How I'd roll it out

  1. Measure first. Compare requests with real usage by namespace and team, using the allocation approach in FOCUS-based cost allocation.
  2. Start with CPU on stateless services, using NotRequired, where the risk is lowest and the savings show quickly.
  3. Run the VPA in recommendation mode for a few weeks, then enable InPlaceOrRecreate on workloads that tolerate the fallback.
  4. Use it for warm-up spikes. Services that need extra CPU at start-up, including model servers like those in vLLM serving, can start large and shrink once warm.
  5. Alert on pending resizes and report status, not spec, in cost dashboards.
  6. Combine with scale-to-zero from Kubernetes FinOps: horizontal scaling for traffic shape, vertical for per-Pod fit.

item.title: Text-to-SQL agents need a semantic layer, not just a bigger model
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: LLMs ace text-to-SQL demos and stumble on real enterprise schemas. What Spider 2.0 showed, why a governed semantic layer helps, and how I design data access for AI agents.
item.content:encoded:
'Ask your data anything' is one of the most requested AI features, and one of the most disappointing in production. The demo works on a tidy schema. The real warehouse has thousands of columns, conflicting definitions and tribal knowledge. Research and the market are converging on the same fix.

Every data team has seen the demo: a business user types "what was revenue by region last quarter?" and the model writes perfect SQL. Then the same tool meets the real warehouse, with three tables that could be "revenue", a region column that changed meaning in 2023, and a fiscal calendar nobody wrote down. The answers come back quickly, confidently and wrong.

What the research shows

Spider 2.0, presented at ICLR 2025, was built from real enterprise workflows: 632 problems over databases often with more than a thousand columns, in systems such as BigQuery and Snowflake. The authors reported that a strong reasoning model using a code agent framework solved 21.3% of tasks, compared with 91.2% on the earlier Spider 1.0 benchmark and 73.0% on BIRD12.

The gap isn't mainly about SQL syntax. It is about knowing which tables matter, what columns mean, how entities join, and which business rules apply. That knowledge rarely lives in the schema.

Text-to-SQL fails on meaning, not grammar. A bigger model writes more fluent wrong queries; a semantic layer gives it the right things to query.

What a semantic layer gives an agent

A semantic layer defines business concepts, such as metrics, dimensions, entities and their relationships, once, in governed code, and exposes them to every tool. For an AI agent, that changes the task from "write SQL against 1,500 columns" to "pick the governed metric 'net revenue', group by the dimension 'sales region', filter to last fiscal quarter". The layer generates the SQL.

  • Consistency. The agent's answer matches the dashboard, because both use the same definition.
  • Smaller search space. Choosing from a curated set of metrics is far easier than reasoning over raw tables.
  • Governance. Access control, row-level security and certified definitions apply to AI queries just as they do to BI.
  • Explainability. The agent can say which metric and filters it used, in business terms a user can check.

The market is converging

In September 2025 Snowflake, Salesforce, dbt Labs and others announced the Open Semantic Interchange, an initiative for a vendor-neutral semantic model specification, explicitly framed around making data ready for AI3. In October 2025 dbt Labs moved MetricFlow, the engine behind its semantic layer, to the Apache 2.0 licence and said it would align it with that initiative45.

Whatever tools you choose, the direction is clear: business definitions are becoming portable, open artefacts that AI and BI share, rather than logic buried in each dashboard.

Semantic layer, ontology or both?

A semantic layer is optimised for metrics: numbers aggregated over dimensions. An ontology describes entities and relationships more broadly, as I set out in ontology vs knowledge graph vs semantic layer. For "how much" questions, the semantic layer is the right tool. For "which suppliers are connected to this incident", a knowledge graph answers better. Mature data platforms give agents both, with clear guidance on which to use.

How I design data access for AI agents

  1. Start with the twenty questions people actually ask, and define the metrics and dimensions they need in the semantic layer first.
  2. Expose governed tools, not a SQL console. Agents call "query metric" and "list dimensions" tools, for example through MCP servers built with the controls in securing MCP servers.
  3. Return the definition with the answer, so users see which metric, filters and time range were used.
  4. Fall back honestly. If a question can't be answered from governed definitions, say so and route it to an analyst, rather than improvising SQL.
  5. Evaluate with real questions and known answers, as in evaluation sets that predict production, and track accuracy by question type.
  6. Keep definitions under contract, with the change discipline in data contracts, so a schema change can't silently break what agents report.
